unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Alderford Kitchens Ltd is a private limited company in Country X, founded 9 years ago, selling and installing fitted kitchens from a showroom and workshop in Redby. It employs 28 staff and generated sales of $3.9 million last year. The business also holds around $1.1 million of showroom stock and unsold fitted units. The average installed kitchen costs $9,400, and around 65% of customers spread the payment over three years using a finance plan arranged by the showroom.

Over the past 12 months, Country X's central bank raised its base rate from 3% to 6% to control inflation of 5.2%. Monthly finance applications fell from 160 to 92, and showroom orders dropped from 200 to 156 last quarter, a fall of 22%. Owner Daniel Reyes must decide how to respond to weakening demand for high-value kitchens.

questions.question_text: Define 'interest rate'.
questions.model_answer: An interest rate is the cost of borrowing money or the reward for saving, expressed as a percentage of the amount borrowed or saved per year. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Interest rate is the cost of borrowing or the reward for saving, expressed as a percentage
Measured on the amount borrowed or saved, usually on an annual basis

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the rise in interest rates has reduced demand for Alderford Kitchens.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive [k]. With the base rate up at 6%, monthly payments on a finance plan for an average $9,400 kitchen have risen, so some customers can no longer afford the repayments and postpone buying [app]. Reason 2: Higher rates increase the reward for saving [k]. With savings now earning more interest, customers prefer to keep their money in the bank rather than commit to a three-year finance plan [app].

knowledge_max_2: Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive, reducing demand for financed purchases
Higher interest rates increase the incentive to save rather than spend
application_max_2: Base rate raised from 3% to 6%; finance plan for an average $9,400 kitchen
Monthly finance applications fell from 160 to 92

questions.question_text: Explain two problems the fall in orders from 200 to 156 causes for Alderford Kitchens.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Lower sales revenue and profit [k]. Orders dropped from 200 to 156 last quarter, a fall of 22%, so fewer kitchens are being sold and income from sales and fitting work has fallen [app], threatening the business's ability to cover fixed costs such as rent and the workshop [an]. Problem 2: Idle staff and wasted capacity [k]. With fewer kitchens to install, the 28 staff across the showroom and workshop in Redby have less work each week [app], so labour costs are spread over fewer jobs and may force the owner to cut hours or make redundancies [an].

knowledge_max_2: Lower revenue and profit threaten the ability to cover fixed costs
Falling output leaves staff and capacity underused
application_max_2: Orders dropped from 200 to 156 last quarter, a fall of 22%
28 staff across the showroom and workshop in Redby; $1.1 million of stock
analysis_max_2: Fixed costs spread over fewer kitchens reduce the profit margin and cash flow
Underused labour raises the average cost per kitchen and may force redundancies or shorter hours

questions.question_text: Do you think Alderford Kitchens should cut the price of an average kitchen to boost demand? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Cutting the price could help win back price-sensitive buyers [k]: showroom orders dropped from 200 to 156 after the base rate rose from 3% to 6% [app], so a 10% price cut might lift volume enough to spread fixed costs over more kitchens and protect the workshop's workload [an]. However, a broad price cut would squeeze profit per kitchen [k]: the average installed kitchen already costs $9,400 and the real barrier is the higher 6% interest on finance plans used by 65% of customers [app], so cheaper prices alone may not restore demand while borrowing stays expensive [an]. Overall [eval], Alderford should avoid a permanent across-the-board price cut and instead offer a time-limited discount or contribution to finance costs [eval], because the fall in orders was driven by borrowing costs rather than the kitchen price itself.

knowledge_max_2: Price cuts can stimulate demand by improving value for money
Cutting prices reduces the profit margin earned on each unit sold
application_max_2: Orders fell from 200 to 156 after the base rate rose from 3% to 6%
Average installed kitchen costs $9,400; 65% of customers use a finance plan
analysis_max_2: Higher volume after a cut spreads fixed costs over more kitchens, lifting margin per period
If the barrier is finance cost, a price cut does not remove it and margins simply fall
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options using stem figures before reaching a justified position
Conditional, justified recommendation (time-limited offer, not a permanent cut)

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Marne Valley Dairies is a family-run dairy farm in Country X, trading for 14 years. It keeps 85 cows, employs 11 workers and sells milk to a regional processing plant under a supply agreement, earning revenue of $820,000 and a profit of $46,000 last year.

Two years ago the farm borrowed $400,000 from its bank at a variable interest rate of 4% to replace its milking parlour. Since then the central bank has raised the base rate to 7%, so annual interest on the loan has risen from $16,000 to $28,000, an extra $12,000 a year. Milk prices have stayed flat while feed and energy costs have risen. Owner Marta Ellison must decide how to manage the loan now that interest rates are much higher.

questions.question_text: Calculate how much more interest the farm pays each year at 7% compared with 4% on its $400,000 loan.
questions.model_answer: At 4% the annual interest is $16,000 and at 7% it is $28,000 [1]; the difference is $28,000 - $16,000 = $12,000 extra a year [1]. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Difference = $12,000 additional interest per year

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why a rise in interest rates increases the financial pressure on businesses with loans.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Higher rates directly raise the cost of borrowing [k]. Marne Valley's annual interest on its $400,000 loan has risen from $16,000 to $28,000, an extra $12,000 a year [app]. Reason 2: Higher interest payments reduce profit and cash flow [k]. The farm's profit was only $46,000 last year, so the extra $12,000 removes over a quarter of its profit before tax or reinvestment [app].

knowledge_max_2: Interest costs rise when variable rates rise, increasing fixed financial commitments
Higher interest payments reduce profit and cash available for investment
application_max_2: Interest risen from $16,000 to $28,000 on the $400,000 variable-rate loan
Profit of $46,000; the extra $12,000 is over a quarter of annual profit

questions.question_text: Explain two ways Marne Valley Dairies could respond to the extra $12,000 annual interest cost.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: Cut production costs [k]. Feed and energy costs have already risen even though milk prices have stayed flat [app], so the farm could trim waste and renegotiate supplier prices to restore the margin [an]. Way 2: Renegotiate the loan with its bank [k]. The $400,000 outstanding loan could be stretched over a longer repayment period or converted to a fixed rate [app], which spreads the cost more evenly and removes the risk of rates rising again [an].

knowledge_max_2: Reducing costs offsets higher interest without cutting sales
Refinancing or renegotiating can spread repayments or fix the rate
application_max_2: Feed and energy costs have risen while milk prices have stayed flat
Variable-rate loan of $400,000; base rate raised to 7%; interest now $28,000 a year
analysis_max_2: Lower costs rebuild the profit margin absorbed by the extra $12,000
A longer term or fixed rate smooths cash flow and caps future repayments

questions.question_text: Do you think Marne Valley Dairies should switch its loan to a fixed rate now? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Switching to a fixed rate would give the farm certainty [k]: at 7.5% the annual interest would be $30,000, only $2,000 more than the $28,000 it pays now [app], so the business can budget with confidence if the base rate rises again [an]. However, a fixed rate removes the benefit if rates fall [k]: if the base rate returns to 4%, the farm would still pay $30,000 instead of $16,000, an extra $14,000 a year [app], which would hurt a farm whose profit is only $46,000 [an]. Overall [eval], with profit so thin and rates already well above the 4% at which the loan was taken, the farm should fix the rate to protect cash flow [eval], accepting a small premium for certainty.

knowledge_max_2: Fixed rate gives certainty of repayments regardless of rate movements
Fixed rate removes the benefit if market interest rates fall
application_max_2: Fixed at 7.5% = $30,000 a year vs $28,000 now, only $2,000 more
If the rate fell back to 4% the farm would pay $14,000 a year extra; profit only $46,000
analysis_max_2: Certainty helps budgeting and protects against further rises
Being locked into a high fixed rate wastes money if rates fall
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options using stem figures before deciding
Reaches a justified, qualified recommendation (fix to protect thin profit and cash flow)

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Harbury Carpets is an independent carpet and flooring retailer in Country X, trading for 11 years from two high-street stores. It employs 19 trained staff, and last year it sold carpets worth $2.7 million, up from $2.35 million the year before. The average fitted carpet costs $1,850, including underlay and fitting.

Nine months ago the central bank cut its base rate from 6% to 4% to boost consumer spending, and the government hopes the cut will restore confidence after a slow year. Since then, applications from customers wanting to spread the cost with finance have risen by 35%, and Harbury's weekly takings have increased by 15%. Owner Sophie Aldana is considering hiring five more sales assistants and increasing stock levels to meet expected demand.

questions.question_text: Define 'base rate'.
questions.model_answer: The base rate is the interest rate set by a country's central bank, which influences the cost of borrowing and the return on savings across the whole economy. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Interest rate set by the central bank
Influences other borrowing and saving interest rates in the economy

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the cut in interest rates has increased demand for Harbury Carpets.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Cheaper finance makes spreading the cost more affordable [k]. Applications from customers wanting to spread the cost with finance have risen by 35% since the base rate was cut from 6% to 4% [app]. Reason 2: Lower borrowing costs leave households with more disposable income [k]. Weekly takings have increased by 15% and sales rose to $2.7 million from $2.35 million [app].

knowledge_max_2: Lower interest rates reduce the cost of finance and loans
Lower borrowing costs increase households' disposable income
application_max_2: Finance applications up 35% after the base rate cut from 6% to 4%
Weekly takings up 15%; sales of $2.7 million vs $2.35 million

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Harbury Carpets of the recent rise in demand.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Higher sales revenue [k]. Sales rose from $2.35 million to $2.7 million last year, an increase of about $350,000 [app], which gives the business more cash to reinvest, stock up or hire staff [an]. Benefit 2: Fixed costs are spread over more output [k]. Selling carpets costing $1,850 each from two high-street stores spreads rent, wages and display costs over more units [app], so the profit margin on each carpet rises as volume grows [an].

knowledge_max_2: Higher sales revenue improves cash flow and profit
Higher output spreads fixed costs, raising the profit margin
application_max_2: Sales rose from $2.35 million to $2.7 million, about $350,000 more
Two high-street stores; average fitted carpet $1,850; 19 trained staff
analysis_max_2: Extra revenue can be reinvested in stock or hiring to sustain growth
Fixed costs shared over more carpets raise the profit earned per sale

questions.question_text: Do you think Harbury Carpets should hire five more sales assistants now? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Hiring five more sales assistants would help the business cope with buoyant demand [k]: takings rose 15% and finance applications jumped 35% after the base rate was cut from 6% to 4% [app], so extra staff can serve the two stores properly, protect service quality and convert more enquiries into sales [an]. However, the recovery may not last [k]: takings grew from $2.35 million to $2.7 million, but demand could fall back if the central bank reverses the cut, leaving the business paying five more salaries [app], so costs would rise faster than sales and profit would fall [an]. Overall [eval], with demand up 15% and two busy stores, hiring part-time assistants first is justified [eval], but Sophie Aldana should review staffing monthly in case the base rate is raised again.

knowledge_max_2: Matching labour capacity to demand supports service and sales conversion
Adding fixed wages raises costs if demand falls back
application_max_2: Takings up 15% and finance applications up 35% after the base rate cut from 6% to 4%
Sales rose from $2.35 million to $2.7 million; two high-street stores; $1,850 average carpet
analysis_max_2: Extra staff convert enquiries into sales and maintain customer service
If rates rise again, idle staff inflate wage costs and erode profit
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options using stem figures and reaches a justified position
Conditional recommendation (hire, ideally part-time first, review monthly)

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Caldermoor Crane Hire Ltd is a private limited company in Country X, operating for 8 years hiring tower cranes and mobile cranes to building firms. It employs 24 staff, including 6 crane operators, and earned $3.1 million in revenue last year.

The company needs to borrow $600,000 to buy two new tower cranes. Its bank offers either a fixed rate of 7.5% for five years, costing $45,000 interest each year, or a variable rate, currently 6% ($36,000 a year), which could rise or fall. The base rate has moved from 5% to 6.5% over the past year, and the central bank has warned that further increases remain possible. Directors must choose between the fixed and variable loans before signing the crane purchase order.

questions.question_text: Define 'fixed rate'.
questions.model_answer: A fixed rate is an interest rate that stays the same for an agreed period of time, so the borrower's repayments do not change even if other interest rates move. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Interest rate held constant for an agreed period
Repayments remain unchanged regardless of market rate movements

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons Caldermoor Crane Hire Ltd may prefer the fixed-rate loan.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Certainty of repayments [k]. At 7.5% the company would pay $45,000 interest each year for five years, a known cost it can budget for regardless of rate movements [app]. Reason 2: Protection against further rate rises [k]. The base rate has moved from 5% to 6.5% over the past year, and the central bank has warned more increases are possible, so fixing now caps the company's exposure [app].

knowledge_max_2: Fixed rate gives certainty of interest costs for planning
Fixed rate protects against future rises in market interest rates
application_max_2: $45,000 interest each year for five years at a fixed rate of 7.5%
Base rate moved from 5% to 6.5% this year; further increases possible

questions.question_text: Explain two ways Caldermoor Crane Hire Ltd could reduce the financial risk of the $600,000 loan.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: Choose the fixed option [k]. Paying $45,000 a year is $9,000 more than the current variable cost of $36,000, but it caps the maximum the company will pay [app], removing the risk of repayments climbing if the base rate rises again [an]. Way 2: Fund part of the purchase from retained profit [k]. Revenue last year was $3.1 million, so saving a deposit towards the two cranes would shrink the amount borrowed [app], which lowers the total interest bill whatever rate is charged [an].

knowledge_max_2: Fixed rate caps exposure to future interest rate rises
Part-funding from retained profit reduces the amount borrowed
application_max_2: $45,000 fixed vs $36,000 variable now, a $9,000 annual premium
Revenue of $3.1 million last year; two new tower cranes needing $600,000
analysis_max_2: Paying a small premium eliminates the risk of much higher repayments later
A smaller principal means lower total interest paid and lower risk

questions.question_text: Do you think Caldermoor Crane Hire Ltd should choose the fixed-rate loan at 7.5% rather than the variable-rate loan at 6%? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Choosing the fixed rate gives Caldermoor certainty [k]: the company would pay $45,000 each year regardless of movements, and the base rate has already climbed from 5% to 6.5% with more increases warned [app], so fixing protects a business with $3.1 million revenue from surprise repayment rises on the $600,000 loan [an]. However, the fixed option costs $9,000 more each year right now [k]: at 6% the variable loan costs just $36,000, and if the base rate stabilises or falls the company would overpay for five years [app], draining cash that could fund crane maintenance or marketing [an]. Overall [eval], with rates rising and the central bank warning of further increases, the fixed loan is the safer choice [eval], provided the extra $9,000 a year does not push cash flow below the level needed to run 24 staff and service the cranes.

knowledge_max_2: Fixed rate removes repayment uncertainty
Variable rate is cheaper initially but can rise unpredictably
application_max_2: $45,000 per year fixed vs $36,000 per year variable (a $9,000 difference)
Base rate moved from 5% to 6.5% with further increases possible; loan of $600,000
analysis_max_2: Certainty protects cash flow and supports budgeting and planning
Overpaying $9,000 a year if rates fall wastes money that could fund operations
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options using stem figures
Justified recommendation with a cash-flow proviso, not a one-sided answer

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Alcott Windows Ltd is a double-glazing and window installer based in Country X, operating for 12 years. It employs 22 staff and generated $2.6 million in revenue last year, installing windows, doors and roofline products for homes and small offices across the region. The business holds $400,000 of window and door stock in its warehouse.

The central bank has raised its base rate from 3.5% to 6.5% over 9 months. Around 75% of Alcott's customers pay by finance plan, and installations have fallen from 120 to 84 per quarter, a drop of 30%. The workshop is running at half its usual capacity. Staff fear job losses, and owner Luis Cabrera must decide how to respond to falling orders and rising finance costs before the summer peak.

questions.question_text: Define 'mortgage'.
questions.model_answer: A mortgage is a long-term loan used to buy property such as a house or flat, repaid with interest over many years and usually secured against the property itself. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Long-term loan used to purchase property
Repaid with interest over many years, typically secured on the property

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why higher interest rates have reduced demand for Alcott Windows.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Finance to spread the cost of windows is now more expensive [k]. Around 75% of Alcott's customers pay by finance plan, and with the base rate up at 6.5% the monthly repayments on new orders have risen [app]. Reason 2: Higher rates leave households with less disposable income [k]. Homeowners face bigger mortgage repayments, so installations have fallen from 120 to 84 per quarter, a drop of 30% [app].

knowledge_max_2: Higher interest rates increase the cost of finance plans
Higher rates raise mortgage costs, reducing disposable income
application_max_2: 75% of customers pay by finance plan; base rate raised to 6.5%
Installations fell from 120 to 84 per quarter, a drop of 30%

questions.question_text: Explain two problems the fall from 120 to 84 installations a quarter causes Alcott Windows.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Lower revenue and profit [k]. A drop of 30% means far fewer windows sold each quarter [app], so fixed costs such as warehouse rent and the interest on $400,000 of stock are spread over fewer jobs, squeezing margins [an]. Problem 2: Under-used labour and capacity [k]. The workshop is running at half its usual capacity, with 22 staff and much of the $400,000 stock sitting unsold [app], so the business may be forced to cut hours or make installers redundant [an].

knowledge_max_2: Falling orders reduce revenue and profit
Falling output leaves labour and stock underutilised
application_max_2: Installations fell from 120 to 84 per quarter, a drop of 30%
$400,000 of stock; workshop at half its usual capacity; 22 staff
analysis_max_2: Fewer sales spread fixed costs over less output, squeezing the profit margin
Idle capacity pressures the business into wage cuts or redundancy

questions.question_text: Do you think Alcott Windows should cut prices by 10% to win back orders? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: A 10% price cut could win back price-sensitive customers [k]: installations have fallen from 120 to 84 per quarter, a drop of 30%, so a discount might persuade cautious homeowners to proceed before the summer peak [app], lifting volume enough to cover fixed warehouse costs on $400,000 of stock [an]. However, the real barrier is the 6.5% base rate, not the price [k]: around 75% of Alcott's customers pay by finance plan, so higher monthly repayments are stopping purchases, not the quoted price [app], meaning a blanket 10% cut would simply reduce margin on the 84 orders still coming in [an]. Overall [eval], Alcott should offer a targeted discount or contribution to finance costs on finance-plan sales rather than a blanket 10% cut [eval], because the demand fall is driven by borrowing costs rather than the headline price.

knowledge_max_2: Price cuts can attract price-sensitive customers
Demand driven by borrowing cost is not resolved by price cuts
application_max_2: Installations fell from 120 to 84 per quarter, a drop of 30%
75% of customers pay by finance plan; base rate raised from 3.5% to 6.5%
analysis_max_2: A discount could lift volume enough to cover fixed costs
Margins on remaining orders fall without fixing the real barrier
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options using stem figures
Justified, conditional recommendation (targeted offer, not a blanket cut)

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Elmcrest Farm Machinery is a tractor and combine dealer in rural Country X, trading for 15 years and supplying an area of about 4,000 square kilometres. It employs 17 staff, sells new and used machines and provides servicing, parts and breakdown cover, earning revenue of $5.4 million last year.

New tractor sales, usually around 120 a year at an average price of $48,000, have fallen to 66 this year after the central bank raised its base rate from 4% to 7%. Most farmers finance purchases with bank loans. To fund showroom stock the dealer uses a $500,000 overdraft, and overdraft interest has risen from 6% to 9%, costing an extra $15,000 a year. Several farmers have asked to defer orders until rates fall.

questions.question_text: Define 'overdraft'.
questions.model_answer: An overdraft is a bank facility that lets a business withdraw more money from its current account than it holds, up to an agreed limit and repaid with interest. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Facility allowing withdrawal beyond the account balance up to an agreed limit
Repayable with interest, often on demand

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why farmers may postpone buying new tractors when interest rates rise.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Loans to buy tractors become more expensive [k]. Most farmers finance purchases with bank loans, and with the base rate up from 4% to 7% the interest on financing a $48,000 tractor has jumped sharply [app]. Reason 2: Farmers are uncertain about future income while rates are high [k]. Tractor sales fell from 120 a year to 66 this year, showing farmers are delaying major capital purchases [app].

knowledge_max_2: Higher interest increases the cost of finance for capital purchases
Uncertainty and low confidence make buyers delay major investments
application_max_2: Base rate raised from 4% to 7%; average tractor price $48,000
New tractor sales fell from 120 a year to 66 this year

questions.question_text: Explain two ways Elmcrest Farm Machinery could reduce the cost of holding stock.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: Reduce showroom stock and order to demand [k]. With sales down to 66 from 120 a year, fewer machines are needed on the forecourt [app], so the dealer can shrink its $500,000 overdraft and cut the interest it pays [an]. Way 2: Renegotiate the overdraft with its bank [k]. Overdraft interest has risen from 6% to 9%, costing an extra $15,000 a year [app], so even a 1% reduction in the margin would save $5,000 a year [an].

knowledge_max_2: Lower stock levels reduce financing needs and interest costs
Renegotiating bank facilities can cut interest margins
application_max_2: Sales fell from 120 a year to 66; overdraft of $500,000
Overdraft interest rose from 6% to 9%, an extra $15,000 a year ($30,000 to $45,000)
analysis_max_2: Less stock directly reduces the overdraft and its interest charge
Even a 1% lower margin yields $5,000 a year and frees working capital

questions.question_text: Do you think Elmcrest Farm Machinery should offer a promotional discount on new tractors to clear stock? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Offering a time-limited discount could clear slow-moving stock [k]: sales fell from 120 a year to 66 this year after the base rate was raised from 4% to 7% [app], so discounting machines would reduce the $500,000 overdraft and the extra $15,000 a year of interest now being paid [an]. However, discounting cuts the margin on each $48,000 tractor and may train buyers to wait for promotions [k]: farmers have already asked to defer orders until rates fall, so a discount might simply shift sales forward rather than create new demand [app], reducing revenue of $5.4 million and further eroding profit [an]. Overall [eval], a modest, time-limited promotional discount is justified [eval], because cutting stock and overdraft interest is worth more than defending the full margin while interest rates remain high.

knowledge_max_2: Promotions stimulate demand and clear excess stock
Discounting reduces margin and can train customers to wait for deals
application_max_2: Sales fell from 120 a year to 66 after the base rate was raised from 4% to 7%
$500,000 overdraft; interest rose from 6% to 9%, an extra $15,000 a year
analysis_max_2: Lower stock cuts overdraft interest and frees working capital
Lower margins and wait-for-discount behaviour reduce profit
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options using stem figures
Justified recommendation (modest, time-limited promotional discount)

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Rowanbrook Ice Cream Co is a private limited company in Country X producing premium ice cream, founded 6 years ago. It employs 34 staff and generated $2.8 million in sales last year, exporting some of its output to two neighbouring countries. Demand has been strong as the economy grows by 4.5% a year.

Inflation has reached 6.5%, well above the government target of 2%, so the central bank raised its base rate from 3% to 6% to cool spending. The company is profitable and carries no debt apart from the planned loan. Rowanbrook wants to build a $900,000 factory extension funded by a bank loan, costing $54,000 in annual interest at 6% and creating 26 new production jobs. Owner Elena Marsh must decide whether to proceed now or wait until rates fall.

questions.question_text: Define 'boom'.
questions.model_answer: A boom is a phase of the business cycle in which the economy is growing rapidly, with high consumer spending, low unemployment and rising incomes and output. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Phase of the business cycle with rapid economic growth
High spending, low unemployment and rising incomes/output

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the central bank may raise interest rates during a boom.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: To control inflation [k]. Inflation has reached 6.5%, well above the government target of 2%, so higher interest rates should cool spending and slow price rises [app]. Reason 2: To reduce excessive borrowing [k]. The economy is growing at 4.5% a year and the base rate was raised from 3% to 6%, so higher rates discourage households and businesses from taking on more debt [app].

knowledge_max_2: Raise rates to bring inflation back towards its target
Raise rates to curb excessive borrowing and credit growth
application_max_2: Inflation at 6.5% compared with the 2% target
Economy growing at 4.5% a year; base rate raised from 3% to 6%

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Rowanbrook Ice Cream Co of the current boom.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Strong sales demand supports growth [k]. The economy is growing by 4.5% a year and Rowanbrook generated $2.8 million in sales last year, exporting some of its output to two neighbouring countries [app], so demand may support the planned factory extension [an]. Benefit 2: Profits can partly fund expansion [k]. The company is profitable and carries no debt apart from the planned loan [app], so it can use retained profit to cover part of the $900,000 cost and borrow less [an].

knowledge_max_2: Strong consumer demand lifts sales and output
Healthy profits and cash flow enable self-financing of investment
application_max_2: Economy growing at 4.5% a year; sales of $2.8 million; exports to two neighbouring countries
Profitable business with no debt apart from the planned loan for the $900,000 extension
analysis_max_2: Strong demand supports the case for extra capacity
Retained profit cuts the amount borrowed and the interest bill

questions.question_text: Do you think Rowanbrook Ice Cream Co should proceed with the $900,000 factory extension now? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Proceeding would capture strong demand at the right time [k]: the economy is growing at 4.5% a year and Rowanbrook sold $2.8 million of ice cream last year [app], so extra capacity would lift output and spread fixed costs, raising the profit on each tub [an]. However, borrowing now is expensive [k]: the base rate was raised from 3% to 6% to cool inflation of 6.5%, and the loan would cost $54,000 a year in interest [app], so if the boom cools the new factory may run below capacity while the interest still has to be paid [an]. Overall [eval], the extension is justified if Rowanbrook fixes the loan rate before it rises further [eval], since strong demand, profitability and no existing debt give the business scope to service the repayments; it should delay only if orders soften before the 26 new jobs are hired.

knowledge_max_2: Investing in capacity during strong demand maximises returns
Borrowing at higher rates increases fixed financial commitments
application_max_2: Economy growing at 4.5% a year; sales of $2.8 million; extension costing $900,000
Base rate raised from 3% to 6%; loan costing $54,000 a year in interest at 6%
analysis_max_2: Extra capacity spreads fixed costs and lifts output and profit
If demand cools, fixed interest must still be paid on below-capacity output
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options using stem figures
Conditional, justified recommendation (proceed with a fixed rate, delay if orders soften)

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Fernwood Café Ltd is a small café in Marrowgate, Country X, trading for 7 years. It employs 12 staff and serves office workers, market shoppers and families, and it is busiest at lunchtimes and weekends. Revenue fell from $420,000 to $330,000 over the last 18 months after two local factories closed with the loss of 240 jobs.

Local unemployment has risen from 4% to 9%, and the central bank cut its base rate from 6% to 3.5% to encourage spending and borrowing. Footfall remains weak despite cheaper credit, and the meal deals introduced in January had little effect. Owner Priya Nandakumar is considering a $150,000 second outlet in a neighbouring town, or staying with one site and trimming staff hours, and she fears opening now could magnify losses.

questions.question_text: Define 'recession'.
questions.model_answer: A recession is a phase of the business cycle in which economic activity falls, usually shown by two consecutive quarters of negative GDP growth, with rising unemployment and falling consumer spending. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Period of falling economic output/negative GDP growth
Rising unemployment and weak consumer spending

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the cut in interest rates from 6% to 3.5% could help Fernwood Café.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Customers can afford to borrow and spend more [k]. Lower rates reduce the cost of personal loans and overdrafts, so office workers and families may return to the café at lunchtimes and weekends [app]. Reason 2: The café could finance a second outlet more cheaply [k]. With the base rate cut to 3.5%, a loan for the $150,000 neighbouring-town outlet would carry much lower interest [app].

knowledge_max_2: Lower rates increase disposable income and the incentive to spend
Lower rates reduce the cost of business borrowing
application_max_2: Base rate cut from 6% to 3.5%; café serves office workers and families
A second outlet costing $150,000 in a neighbouring town

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Fernwood Café may still struggle despite cheaper credit.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Consumer confidence is low and unemployment is high [k]. Local unemployment has risen from 4% to 9% after two local factories closed with the loss of 240 jobs [app], so even cheap credit may not persuade cautious households to eat out [an]. Reason 2: The café's revenue has already collapsed [k]. Revenue fell from $420,000 to $330,000 over the last 18 months [app], so fixed costs such as rent and the wages of 12 staff are spread over far fewer customers, squeezing profit [an].

knowledge_max_2: Low confidence and high unemployment suppress spending regardless of rates
Falling revenue against unchanged fixed costs erodes profit
application_max_2: Unemployment rose from 4% to 9%; two factories closed with 240 jobs lost
Revenue fell from $420,000 to $330,000 over 18 months; 12 staff
analysis_max_2: Fearful households save rather than spend, so the rate cut has limited effect
Fixed costs spread over fewer sales reduce margin and risk losses

questions.question_text: Do you think Fernwood Café should open the second outlet now? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Opening now would give Fernwood a foothold in a neighbouring town before the market recovers [k]: a loan at the cut base rate of 3.5% would be relatively cheap for the $150,000 cost [app], and capturing customers early could help rebuild revenue towards the $420,000 it earned before the closures [an]. However, the café is already weakened by the recession [k]: revenue has fallen from $420,000 to $330,000 and local unemployment has risen to 9% with 240 jobs lost in two factory closures [app], so taking on $150,000 of new commitments while one site struggles could magnify losses and threaten the original café [an]. Overall [eval], Fernwood should wait rather than open now [eval], because opening in a recession with weak footfall and collapsed revenue risks compounding losses; it should hold the $150,000 and focus on restoring sales at the existing site.

Expanding while loss-making multiplies financial risk

Revenue fell from $420,000 to $330,000; unemployment rose to 9%; 240 jobs lost

New fixed commitments in a downturn magnify losses at the existing site

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Corvale Deliveries Ltd is a regional parcel and grocery delivery firm in Country X, trading for 10 years. It employs 29 staff and serves over 300 business customers, running a fleet of 8 diesel vans bought three years ago with a $240,000 bank loan secured against the vehicles. Revenue was $1.9 million last year.

The base rate has risen from 3% to 6%, so annual interest on the van loan has risen from $7,200 to $14,400, an extra $7,200 a year. Inflation has reached 7%, pushing diesel and wage costs higher, and the fuel bill rose by $38,000 last year. Customers resist surcharges. Owner Aaron Bell must decide whether to raise delivery prices by 8% across all contracts or absorb the extra costs and cut other expenses.

questions.question_text: Define 'inflation'.
questions.model_answer: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level of goods and services, which reduces the purchasing power of money over time. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Sustained rise in the general price level
Reduces the purchasing power of money (each unit buys less)

questions.question_text: Explain two problems rising inflation causes for Corvale Deliveries.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Diesel and wage costs rise faster than revenue [k]. Inflation has reached 7%, the fuel bill rose by $38,000 last year, and wages must keep pace to retain the firm's 29 staff [app]. Reason 2: Pressure on margins because customers resist surcharges [k]. Interest on the $240,000 van loan is also up $7,200 a year after the base rate rose from 3% to 6%, so the gap between costs and revenue keeps widening [app].

knowledge_max_2: Inflation raises input costs such as fuel and wages
Inflation forces higher prices or squeezes profit margins
application_max_2: Inflation at 7%; fuel bill rose by $38,000; 29 staff
Interest on the $240,000 van loan up $7,200 a year after the base rate rose from 3% to 6%

questions.question_text: Explain two ways Corvale Deliveries could respond to its rising costs.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: Raise delivery prices to customers [k]. An 8% increase across all contracts would recover some of the extra $7,200 a year of interest and the $38,000 fuel increase [app], though the firm risks losing rounds to cheaper rivals [an]. Way 2: Improve route efficiency and cut empty miles [k]. Combining parcel routes across its 300-plus business customers would cut diesel use per drop [app], lowering costs without raising prices [an].

knowledge_max_2: Passing costs on through higher prices restores margin
Efficiency improvements reduce cost per unit delivered
application_max_2: Proposed 8% increase across all contracts; extra $7,200 interest; $38,000 fuel rise
300-plus business customers; 8 diesel vans; 29 staff
analysis_max_2: Higher prices recover costs but risk losing contracts to rivals
Better route planning cuts fuel burn, protecting margin without price rises

questions.question_text: Do you think Corvale Deliveries should raise its delivery prices by 8% across all contracts? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Raising prices would protect the firm's margin [k]: inflation has reached 7%, the fuel bill rose by $38,000 last year and interest on the $240,000 van loan is up $7,200 a year [app], so an 8% rise across all contracts would broadly recover these quantified extra costs [an]. However, a flat 8% rise risks losing price-sensitive contracts [k]: customers resist surcharges and rivals that hold prices could win the firm's rounds [app], so Corvale could lose more revenue than it recovers [an]. Overall [eval], Corvale should raise prices by a smaller, cost-linked amount rather than a flat 8%, or add a transparent fuel surcharge [eval], because recovering proven cost increases is fairer and less likely to drive away the 300-plus business customers it serves.

knowledge_max_2: Higher prices recover rising input costs
Flat across-the-board rises risk driving customers to rivals
application_max_2: Inflation at 7%; fuel bill up $38,000; interest up $7,200 on the $240,000 loan
Customers resist surcharges; 8% proposed across all contracts
analysis_max_2: An 8% rise broadly offsets the quantified cost increases
Losing contracts could outweigh the recovered costs
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options using stem figures
Justified, qualified recommendation (smaller cost-linked rise or fuel surcharge)

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Eldercombe Toys Ltd is a toy manufacturer in Country X, trading for 18 years. It employs 41 staff across moulding, painting and packing, and sold $3.4 million of toys in a recent boom year. In the slump that followed, sales fell to $2.6 million and profit dropped to $120,000. Around a third of output is exported.

The central bank cut its base rate from 6% to 3%, and the economy is growing again at 2.8% a year. The Christmas period accounts for 55% of annual sales, and retailers are rebuilding stock, so orders are rising. The planned $350,000 expansion would add a new moulding machine and 6 jobs. Owner Hannah Doyle must choose between expanding capacity now or keeping it unchanged until the recovery is confirmed.

questions.question_text: Define 'business cycle'.
questions.model_answer: The business cycle is the regular pattern of economic growth and decline over time, moving through phases of growth, boom, recession and slump. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Regular pattern of economic expansion and contraction
Phases include growth, boom, recession and slump

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why businesses may cut output and staff numbers during a slump.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Consumer demand and sales fall [k]. Eldercombe's sales fell from $3.4 million in the boom year to $2.6 million in the slump, so producing at full capacity would create unsold stock and waste [app]. Reason 2: Falling profits force cost-cutting [k]. Profit dropped to $120,000 in the slump, so reducing staff hours and output was necessary to avoid losses [app].

knowledge_max_2: A slump reduces consumer demand for goods
Falling profits force businesses to cut costs, including labour
application_max_2: Sales fell from $3.4 million to $2.6 million
Profit dropped to $120,000

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Eldercombe Toys of the economy moving from slump to recovery.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Rising orders as retailers rebuild stock [k]. The economy is growing at 2.8% a year and Christmas accounts for 55% of annual sales [app], so demand should rise sharply in the coming months and Eldercombe can sell more toys [an]. Benefit 2: Cheaper borrowing for expansion [k]. The base rate was cut from 6% to 3% [app], so financing even part of the $350,000 moulding-line expansion would cost less interest than before [an].

knowledge_max_2: Recovery increases consumer and retailer demand
Lower base rates reduce the cost of borrowing
application_max_2: Economy growing at 2.8% a year; Christmas accounts for 55% of sales; retailers rebuilding stock
Base rate cut from 6% to 3%; expansion costing $350,000
analysis_max_2: Higher demand spreads fixed costs and lifts output and profit
Cheaper credit reduces the interest cost of the expansion and improves returns

questions.question_text: Do you think Eldercombe Toys should expand its production capacity now? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Expanding now positions Eldercombe for the Christmas peak [k]: the economy is growing at 2.8% a year, orders are rising as retailers rebuild stock and Christmas accounts for 55% of annual sales [app], so the new moulding machine added by the $350,000 expansion could lift output, spread fixed costs and raise profit [an]. However, the recovery is not guaranteed [k]: in the last slump sales fell from $3.4 million to $2.6 million and profit dropped to $120,000 [app], so committing $350,000 before the recovery is confirmed could leave Eldercombe with idle capacity and 6 extra jobs it cannot sustain [an]. Overall [eval], Eldercombe should expand, but cautiously [eval], by fixing any finance at the current 3% base rate and timing the expansion to be ready before Christmas, because the recovery evidence and cheap credit outweigh the residual risk.

knowledge_max_2: Expanding into rising demand captures sales and market share
Committing capital before recovery is confirmed is risky
application_max_2: Economy growing at 2.8% a year; Christmas accounts for 55% of sales; retailers rebuilding stock; $350,000 expansion
Sales fell from $3.4 million to $2.6 million in the slump; profit dropped to $120,000
analysis_max_2: Extra capacity captures peak demand, raising output, resource utilisation and profit
Idle capacity plus 6 extra jobs in a renewed slump would erode profit
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options using stem figures
Justified recommendation (expand cautiously, timed for Christmas and fixed finance)
